preference_rationale: The devil is in the details. Signals that have been published about for years and commoditized by vendors have likely decayed, but that is decay, not death - there are still opportunities for alpha on top of an existing model given careful construction and discipline about overfitting. What I liked about B is the simple-first approach, but in this case the remaining alpha is probably in the more niche cases that have not been arbed away yet, and a single pooled specification is aimed at the average effect rather than those pockets. This firm has the time and resources, so may as well see how much performance is there. The real-life constraint layering is also critical to building a defensible signal, and that is where A is much stronger.
critique_A:
Kitchen-sink approach, which I would avoid. It is better to start with strong priors and the subsets of the data and the market where you think the signal will work, and test those, than to fit everything and orthogonalize afterward.

The custom-trained transformer might not be needed. FinBERT, or even a time-series z-score fed to a standard scoring model, may get most of the way. A names FinBERT as a baseline to beat but still leads with the domain-adaptation build rather than establishing first what the cheap measure delivers.

The real knock: A does not use a vendor-provided score as the threshold a custom signal has to clear. If a licensed score already captures most of the effect, the custom build is only worth its cost if it beats that score, and A never sets the hurdle.

The constraint layering - spread, impact, ADV caps, borrow, break-even cost, capacity where net alpha halves - is right, and is what makes a signal defensible to this committee.
critique_B:
Simple-first is the right instinct and it is B's best feature.

But B treats commoditization as close to dispositive: vendor availability implies crowding, therefore expect a null. That confuses decay with death. A published signal can still carry alpha for someone constructing it more carefully, and B never tests that possibility.

Where the residual alpha most likely lives is in niche cases not yet arbed away, and B cannot see them. One pooled specification with industry-by-quarter fixed effects estimates the average effect; killing the project at a t of 2.1 on that specification says little about whether pockets survive.

Constraint layering is thin - a flat 20bp round-trip, no borrow cost, no ADV cap, no capacity estimate. For a firm judged on whether a signal survives costs and has capacity, that is not a defensible net number.
why_loser_was_defensible: B's three days of literature and vendor calls before touching returns is genuinely good sequencing, and its vendor rank-correlation control is the exact test A is missing. An analyst who believed the signal was fully arbitraged would rationally spend three days finding out rather than ten weeks building an encoder.
